title: The cell grows sweet (I.20)
hook: love solitude and silence; the cell often kept becomes sweet
tomorrow: if everyone carries sorrow, why does everyone else look fine?

segments.voice: Yesterday: be patient with other people's faults, since they're bearing with ours, and nobody is enough alone. The line was you have yours.

A bedroom on a Saturday, door shut. No plans, no game, phone face down. To some people that's a reset. To others it looks like hiding. The Imitation takes a side, and makes a promise: a small room, kept often, grows sweet. In a monastery that room is called a cell, a monk's or a nun's bed, desk and window. Nothing happens there. That, the book says, is the point. But not every Catholic voice puts the weight in the same place.
screen: `A SHUT DOOR ON A SATURDAY.` → `RESET, OR HIDING?` → `A ROOM THAT GROWS SWEET.`

segments.voice: First, the case for the cell. Chapter twenty of book one says: look for a fitting time to be alone, and think often about God's kindness. It's easier to keep quiet altogether, it says, than not to say too much, and easier to stay home than to guard yourself out in the world. Jesus gives the same gesture in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." Then the promise: the cell, kept often, grows sweet; kept badly, it breeds weariness. A room you come back to stops being empty and becomes a friend. Now the other view, and it's Catholic too. Other saints went out the door instead: to the sick, the poor, the classroom, the street. In the same Gospel, Jesus says that whatever is done for the least of his brothers is done for him. On that reading, service is its own kind of prayer, and a shut door can turn into a hiding place. Some readers hear the Imitation as a book for monks and want it balanced by the works of mercy. The Church keeps both: communities that stay in and pray, and communities that go out and serve. And the Imitation's own promise carries a quiet condition. The cell grows sweet when it's kept for God, not for escape.
screen: `ALONE, AT A FITTING TIME.` · `SHUT THE DOOR.` · `THE CASE FOR GOING OUT.` · `KEPT FOR GOD, NOT FOR ESCAPE.` · then, large: `THE CELL GROWS SWEET.`

segments.voice: Choose one quiet spot you could come back to, a chair, a corner, a window, and sit there now with your phone in another room. Listen for the smallest sound in it, a fan, a bird, the house settling, and stay with that one sound, even when nothing else happens. If you pray, you can let the shut door be your prayer.
The cell grows sweet. The Imitation's promise for a quiet place: kept often, it turns from empty to friendly.
Pocket this one: the cell grows sweet, and it's sweetest when you come back out kinder. Rest well.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns in contemplative orders keep times of silence and spend time in their cells for prayer and reading, while active orders serve in schools, hospitals and parishes; lay Catholics often keep a prayer corner at home or make silent retreats.

notes: Imitation I.20 paraphrased: seek a fit time to be alone and think often of God's benefits; it is easier to be wholly silent than not to exceed in words, easier to keep at home than to guard oneself abroad; the cell continually dwelt in grows sweet, ill kept it breeds weariness. Confirm.

Matthew 6:6 Douay-Rheims: 'But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret...' Confirm the quoted portion. The link between the Imitation's 'shut thy door' and Matthew 6:6 is an allusion.
